name: Linking facts to the issues they bear on
about: Four disputes, each with the issues as stated at intake and the facts as the parties' papers state them. Each fact lists the issues it bears on; some bear on none (background a reviewer need not see under any issue), some on two. Written for ELI Legal's evaluation; no fact is drawn from a real matter.

issues.I1: Whether time for delivery was of the essence of the Supply Agreement
issues.I2: Whether the Claimant validly terminated the Supply Agreement by its notice of 28 April 2023
issues.I3: Whether the Respondent is liable for the losses claimed for late delivery

facts.text: Clause 4.2 provided that the turbines would be delivered to the Claimant's yard no later than 14 March 2023.
The Claimant's procurement manager wrote on 2 February 2023 that the March date was critical because the vessel charter began on 20 March.
The first consignment arrived on 11 April 2023, four weeks after the agreed date.
On 28 April 2023 the Claimant sent a letter stating that it was bringing the agreement to an end with immediate effect.
The letter of 28 April 2023 did not refer to any earlier warning or give the Respondent further time to deliver.
The Respondent replied on 2 May 2023 that it regarded the letter as a repudiation and reserved its rights.
The Claimant paid €84,000 to extend the vessel charter by three weeks.
The Claimant also claims €212,500 for lost profit on a maintenance contract it says it could not perform.
The Respondent's factory was closed for nine days in February 2023 because of a fire in the paint shop.
The parties had dealt with each other since 2017 under a series of annual purchase orders.
The Respondent's sales director accepted in cross-examination that he knew the turbines were needed for a particular vessel.
The Respondent says the Claimant did nothing to source turbines from another supplier.
The Supply Agreement is governed by the law of Examplia.
Clause 9 allowed either party to end the agreement on 30 days' written notice for a material breach that was not remedied.

issues.J1: Whether the reason for the Claimant's dismissal was her capability
issues.J2: Whether the dismissal was fair in all the circumstances
issues.J3: Whether the Claimant was dismissed because she made protected disclosures

facts.text: The Claimant's monthly sales figures fell below target in each of the six months before her dismissal.
She was placed on a performance improvement plan in January 2024 with a review date of 31 March 2024.
No review meeting was ever held under the improvement plan.
On 12 February 2024 she emailed the finance director that invoices were being backdated to hit quarterly targets.
The finance director forwarded her email to the managing director the same afternoon.
She was dismissed by letter dated 4 March 2024, which gave poor performance as the reason.
She was not invited to a meeting before the decision was taken and was not offered an appeal.
The managing director told a colleague that she had become a problem after the February email.
The Respondent employs about 40 people and has no human resources department.
The Claimant had worked for the Respondent for six years and had never been warned.
Her contract provided for a car allowance of £450 a month.
Two other sales staff with lower figures kept their jobs.
The Claimant started a new job on 1 August 2024 at a lower salary.

issues.K1: Whether the Respondent was obliged to erase the Claimant's personal data when he asked
issues.K2: Whether the Respondent notified the personal data breach in time
issues.K3: Whether the Claimant is entitled to compensation for distress

facts.text: On 3 May 2024 the Claimant asked the Respondent in writing to delete everything it held about him.
The Respondent replied that it had to keep his account history for seven years for tax purposes.
His marketing profile and browsing history were still held on 1 October 2024.
On 9 June 2024 an employee's laptop holding an unencrypted copy of the customer database was stolen from a car.
The Respondent's IT manager learned of the theft on 10 June 2024.
The Respondent informed the regulator of the incident on 19 June 2024.
Customers were told about the theft by email on 2 July 2024.
The Claimant says he received phishing messages using his name and order history in July 2024.
His doctor recorded that he was suffering from anxiety and poor sleep.
The Respondent has 1.2 million customers in twelve countries.
The Respondent offered the Claimant a €50 voucher by way of apology.
The Claimant had agreed to receive marketing emails when he opened his account in 2019.

issues.L1: Whether the tribunal had jurisdiction over the claim under the second contract
issues.L2: Whether the tribunal failed to deal with the Applicant's limitation defence
issues.L3: Whether the Applicant lost its right to object by taking part in the arbitration

facts.text: The first contract contained an arbitration clause; the second contract, signed in 2021, gave the courts of Examplia exclusive jurisdiction.
The Respondent's notice of arbitration referred to both contracts.
In its statement of defence the Applicant argued that the claim was brought more than six years after the cause of action accrued.
The award does not mention the time bar argument.
The Applicant filed its defence and attended the hearing without saying that the tribunal lacked power over the second contract.
The Applicant first raised the point about the second contract in its closing submissions.
The hearing lasted four days in Examplia City in March 2025.
The tribunal awarded the Respondent €1.9 million plus interest.
Procedural Order No. 2 directed that every objection to jurisdiction be raised in the statement of defence.
The presiding arbitrator had sat with the Respondent's counsel in two unrelated cases.
The tribunal's reasons on the second contract run to one paragraph.
